q: In an AVL tree, what values may the balance factor (height of left subtree − height of right subtree) take at every node?
options: 0 only
Any value, as long as the root is balanced
explain: AVL trees allow the two subtree heights to differ by at most one, at every node. Reaching ±2 triggers a rotation.

q: Keys 30, 20, 10 are inserted into an empty AVL tree. Which rotation happens, and what is the root afterwards?
options: LL case: a right rotation at 30; the root becomes 20
RR case: a left rotation at 30; the root becomes 10
LR case: a double rotation; the root becomes 10
No rotation; the root stays 30
explain: After inserting 10, node 30 has balance +2 and the new key went left, then left. A single right rotation at 30 makes 20 the root with children 10 and 30.

q: Keys 10, 30, 20 are inserted into an empty AVL tree. Which case is this?
options: RL: right rotation at 30, then left rotation at 10
RR: one left rotation at 10
LR: left rotation at 30, then right rotation at 10
LL: one right rotation at 10
explain: 10 has balance −2, and the path to the new key goes right (to 30), then left (to 20): a zig-zag. Straighten it with a right rotation at 30, then left-rotate at 10. The root becomes 20.

q: After an insertion unbalances an AVL tree, at which node is the rotation applied?
options: The lowest node on the insertion path whose balance factor becomes ±2
Always the root
The parent of the inserted node
The highest node whose balance factor changed
explain: Fixing the lowest unbalanced node restores that subtree to its original height, so every ancestor above it becomes balanced again automatically.

q: How many rotations does a single insertion into an AVL tree need, at most?
options: 2 (one double rotation)
O(log n)
O(n)
explain: One fix, single or double, at the lowest unbalanced node is enough after an insertion. Deletion is different: it may need a rotation at several ancestors.

q: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 4 (height counted in edges, so a single node has height 0)?
explain: N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2 gives 1, 2, 4, 7, 12. So a height-4 AVL tree needs at least 12 nodes.

q: The keys 1, 2, 3, …, 7 are inserted in increasing order into an empty AVL tree. What is the height of the result?
explain: The rotations keep rebalancing, and the result is the perfectly balanced tree with root 4, children 2 and 6, and leaves 1, 3, 5, 7. That has height 2. A plain BST would have height 6.

q: A rotation in an AVL tree changes the inorder sequence of the keys.
explain: False. Rotations only restructure the tree. Every key in the moved subtree T lies between the two rotated nodes, so BST order, and therefore the inorder sequence, is unchanged.

q: Why is the height of an AVL tree with n nodes O(log n)?
options: The minimum number of nodes for height h grows like the Fibonacci numbers, which is exponential in h
Because all its leaves are on the same level
Because each node has exactly two children
Because rotations happen at every insertion
explain: N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 grows exponentially, so h ≤ about 1.44 log₂ n. AVL leaves need not all be on one level.

q: During a right rotation at z (with left child y), what happens to y's right subtree T?
options: It becomes z's new left subtree
It becomes y's left subtree
It is deleted
It becomes z's right subtree
explain: Every key in T is greater than y and smaller than z. After y moves up and z becomes y's right child, T fits exactly as z's left subtree.
